prime.problem: Inference performance advice is a pile of tricks: batch more, quantize, use GQA, buy a bigger GPU. Without one formula to hang them on, you can't tell which trick helps your case, and many help nothing at all.
prime.fits: The map for course 1, read first as a map or last as a recap. It assumes only the series map. Every card after it fills in one symbol of T_step ≈ max(2·N·T ÷ C, (N·b + Σ S·k) ÷ W).
prime.goal: Place every card of the course on one formula, and say for any proposed change which side of the max() it acts on and whether it will help.

attend: Which symbols in the formula come from the model, and which from the chip?
A 1,000-token prefill is math-bound and one decode token is memory-bound. Which single symbol changed between the two?
Why does batching have the biggest bar in the levers table, and what eventually stops it?
Why do more FLOPs help prefill but not batch-1 decode?
Where does the one-formula picture break: MoE, long context, or tiny operations?

must: Each token needs ≈ 2N FLOPs and each step reads all N·b weight bytes plus the KV cache → step time ≈ max(math, memory) → which side wins depends on tokens per weight read vs the chip's ops:byte (295 on an H100)
Prefill: 1,000 tokens share one weight read → math 16.2 ms beats memory 4.8 ms → compute-bound, sets TTFT; decode: 1 token per read → 16.2 µs of math vs 4.79 ms of reading → memory-bound, sets TPOT

Decode is memory-bound → the levers that help cut bytes (FP8 2×, GQA 4× on KV), share each read (batching: 207 → 16,870 tok/s total) or add bandwidth (M3 → H100, 33.5×) → more FLOPs change nothing until the batch passes ≈ 295
KV bytes grow with context × batch → HBM fills (≈ 59 sequences of 8k) before the math side wins; attention FLOPs also grow with context (+27% at 8k) → the simple 2N picture needs its context terms
elevated: MoE: N means active parameters in the math and per-token bytes, but total parameters for memory capacity
Real systems reach only part of peak (about 80–85% of spec FLOPs on H100s) → every number on this card is a floor, not a prediction
reference: the log-scale bar widths in the levers table

compress.prompt: Course level: close all the cards and draw the whole course's causal map: model config → parameters N and KV bytes k (forward pass, attention) → FLOPs 2N (FLOPs card) and bytes N·b + Σ S·k → the chip's C and W (GPU card) → max() and the ridge (roofline) → prefill = TTFT, decode = TPOT (your Mac) → batching, SLOs and goodput (serving). Put one real number on each arrow.
checklist: N = 8.03B → 16.06 GB in BF16; k = 128 KiB per token thanks to GQA
2N = 16.06 GFLOP per token, more at long context
prefill ≈ 16.2 ms (compute) → TTFT; decode ≈ 4.79 ms (memory) → TPOT, ≈ 209 tok/s ceiling
batching raises tokens per read until the SLO, the KV memory or the ridge stops it
the M3 shows the same split (188 vs 14 tok/s) at 1/33 of the bandwidth

retrieve.q: Using the formula, explain in two sentences why buying a GPU with more FLOPs is the wrong fix for slow single-user decode.
answer: at batch 1 the memory term (4.79 ms) is about 295× the math term (16.2 µs)
raising C shrinks only the term that was already tiny, so the max doesn't move
the fix must shrink N·b, the KV bytes, or raise W

retrieve.q: Fill in the formula for one decode token and for a 1,000-token prefill of Llama-3.1-8B BF16 on an H100. Which side wins in each?
Rank four levers for a batch-1 decode service: FP8 weights, GQA instead of MHA, moving to an H200, faster tensor cores. Name the symbol each acts on, and say which does nothing.
answer: GQA shrinks k: small at short context, large at long context (512 → 128 KiB per token)
faster tensor cores raise C: no change to batch-1 decode

compare.q: The overview's formula is the roofline applied to a whole model step. What does the model-step version add, and what does the roofline card show that this one-liner hides?
answer: it adds the model: T tokens per step, N·b weight bytes, and the per-sequence KV term
the roofline card shows intensity vs ridge for any operation, and how batching moves a point
it also lists the limits: caches, CUDA-core work (ridge ≈ 20), launch overhead, imperfect overlap

compare.q: This course puts the KV bytes inside the max() with the weights; the next course's overview adds them outside it. Why is that the more accurate form, and what changes in your predictions?
answer: KV reads are per sequence and never shared by batching, so attention stays memory-bound at any batch
only the weight side chooses between reading and math
so step time keeps growing with batch × context even past the ridge, and KV memory usually caps the batch first

predict.q: A team moves from Llama-3.1-8B to an MoE with 37B active of 671B total parameters (ignore that it needs several GPUs). Before reading on: which symbols in the formula change, and is batch-1 decode still memory-bound?
predict.answer: N in the math term becomes 37B active (74 GFLOP per token), and at batch 1 the bytes read per token also follow the active experts, while memory capacity must hold all 671B. Both sides grow about 4.6× from the dense 8B, so batch-1 decode is still memory-bound. The formula still works once you use active parameters for work and bytes per token, and total parameters for capacity.

apply.task: Pick four rows of the levers table and recompute each from the formula yourself: the FP8 decode floor, how many 8k sequences fit on an H100 with MHA vs GQA-8, the M3 vs H100 batch-1 decode ceilings, and a 1,000-token prefill on CUDA cores (66 TF/s) vs tensor cores (990).
apply.done: You get 4.79 → 2.40 ms; 14 vs 59 sequences; 6.2 vs 209 tok/s; 243 vs 16.2 ms, all matching the table's before → after column.
apply.hint: Free HBM is 80 − 16.06 = 63.9 GB; an 8k sequence is 8,192 × 512 KiB (MHA) or × 128 KiB (GQA-8).
